extracted.intended_audience: Users of the computer algebra system Singular (researchers, advanced students, and practitioners doing computational algebra / invariant theory / polynomial system solving)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and rules-of-thumb for performing algebraic computations in Singular: computing invariant rings, GIT-fans, (non-)commutative Groebner bases, solving polynomial systems symbolically/numerically, and choosing monomial/module/matrix orderings and options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary invariants (non-modular case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the non-modular case secondary invariants are calculated by finding a basis (in terms of monomials) of the base ring modulo the primary invariants, mapping to invariants with the Reynolds operator and using those or their power products such that they are linearly independent modulo the primary invariants (see Kemper and Steel...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute a monomial basis of the base ring modulo the primaries, apply the Reynolds operator to obtain invariants, and select those (or their power products) that remain linearly independent modulo the primaries. See 'Some Algorithms in Invariant Theory of Finite Groups' (Kemper & Steel) for algorithmic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary invariants (modular case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the modular case they are generated according to 'Calculating Invariant Rings of Finite Groups over Arbitrary Fields' by Kemper (J. Symb. Comput. 21, No.3, 351-366, 1996).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the generation method described by Kemper for modular settings (reference provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: SINGULAR invariant_ring behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: SINGULAR's invariant_ring returns 2 matrices, the first containing primary invariants and the second secondary invariants; the third result are the irreducible secondary invariants if the Molien series was available. invariant_ring_random is an alternative method (uses random numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invariant_ring(A) to get primary and secondary invariants; inspect B(1), B(2), B(3) as returned. To use randomized approach, call invariant_ring_random(A,seed) (example uses random numbers between -1 and 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute GIT-fans with gitfan.lib using symmetries and parallelism
rubrics_metrics.description: The library gitfan.lib implements an efficient algorithm for computing GIT-fans, which makes use of symmetries. The algorithm relies on Groebner basis techniques, convex geometry and actions of finite symmetry groups and is suitable for parallel computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LIB "gitfan.lib"; setcores(n); construct J and Q and call GITfan(J,Q). Each cone is represented by a single integer. Exploiting group symmetries reduces computation; the algorithm is appropriate for parallel runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use GAP for orbit decomposition when Singular is slow
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a procedure to compute the orbit decomposition of the group action on the simplex of variables is provided, this is not fast in Singular. It is particularly useful to use GAP to obtain the orbit decomposition and then continue with this data in Singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run GAP scripts (e.g., orbits.gp) to compute simplex orbit representatives, then import results (files like doc/simplexOrbitRepresentativesG25.sing, doc/simplexSymmetryGroupG25.sing, doc/elementsInTermsOfGeneratorsG25.sing) into Singular and use provided procedures (afaces, fullDimImages, computeAfaceOrbits, etc.) to continue the GIT-fan computation efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Left vs two-sided Groebner bases (Singular:Plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: The command std computes a left Groebner basis of a left module generated by a set S. The command twostd computes a two-sided Groebner basis (which is in particular also a left Groebner basis) of a two-sided ideal generated by S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose std when computing left Groebner bases (modules), and twostd when a two-sided ideal Groebner basis is required. See the referenced sections for plural-specific details and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute completely reduced minimal bases (redSB, redTail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set option(redSB) and option(redTail) to make Singular compute completely reduced minimal bases of ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable these options before std/twostd to obtain completely reduced minimal bases. See options documentation for exact semantics and examples (they are used in the non-commutative examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show protocol for long computations (prot option)
rubrics_metrics.description: For long running computations, it is always recommended to set option(prot) to make Singular display some information on the performed computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn option(prot) on to get progress/protocol messages (example uses option(prot) during a lengthy std computation). Use option(noprot) to turn it off again. Refer to Section 5.1.108 for interpretation of displayed symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare ideals and read vector-space dimensions (reduce and vdim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vdim to read off the information on the vector space dimension of factor modules A/L and A/T. Use the command reduce to compare left ideals generated by different bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute L = std(S) and T = twostd(S), then use vdim(L) and vdim(T) to see dimensions of A/L and A/T. Use reduce(L,T) and reduce(T,L) to see whether one basis lies in the ideal generated by the other and to identify non-zero remainders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute right Groebner bases and right syzygies via opposite algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Right-sided computations can be done using the left-sided functionality and opposite algebras: define the opposite algebra Aop, compute left Groebner bases and syzygies there, and transfer (oppose) computed objects back to A to obtain right Groebner bases and right syzygies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workflow: define Aop = opposite(A); setring Aop; compute RIop = std(Iop) and RSop = syz(Iop); setring A; RI = oppose(Aop,RIop) yields the right Groebner basis in A; RS = oppose(Aop,RSop) yields the right syzygy module. Use examples for verification (compute T = matrix(I)*RS and check zeros).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic-numerical approach for solving polynomial systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine numerical methods with a symbolic preprocessing: invest computing power to derive additional knowledge on the geometric structure of the set of solutions to make numerical methods more stable and reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbolic preprocessing (Groebner bases, radical, triangular decomposition, primary decomposition, factorizing Buchberger) to simplify the system, reduce unwanted multiplicities/components, or decompose into smaller problems before applying numerical solvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for symbolic preprocessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on whether we want to preserve multiplicities or not, possible goals for a symbolic preprocessing are: to find another system of generators (for instance, a reduced Groebner basis) for the ideal I; alternatively, find a system of polynomials defining an ideal which has the same radical as I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose preprocessing to match intended numerical treatment: preserve multiplicities when needed, or compute generators of an ideal with the same radical to remove multiplicities. See Sect. A.2 and D.4.21.12 for methods (std, radical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose systems into smaller systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose the system into several smaller (or at least more accessible) systems of polynomial equations; then the set of solutions of the original system is the union of the solution sets of the new systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain decompositions via triangular decomposition (triang lib), the factorizing Buchberger algorithm (facstd), or primary decomposition (primdec lib). After decomposition, solve each component separately and take the union of solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove unwanted (excess) solution components by saturation
rubrics_metrics.description: The equational modelling of a problem frequently causes unwanted solutions (for instance, zero as a multiple solution). To get rid of those, compute the saturation of I with respect to an ideal having the excess components as set of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sat(si,maxideal(...)) or sat(I, J) to remove components supported on a given ideal; example removes the origin as a multiple solution via saturation with the maximal ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce generator count with interred before expensive computations
rubrics_metrics.description: For systems with a large number of generators, the first step in a Singular computation could be to reduce the number of generators by applying the interred command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call interred on the input ideal to drop redundant generators and thereby speed up later Groebner/solving steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use solve.lib and triang.lib for symbolic-numeric solving
rubrics_metrics.description: The Singular libraries solve.lib and triang.lib provide several commands for solving systems of polynomial equations (based on a symbolic-numerical approach via Groebner bases, resp. resultants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example workflow: compute a lex Groebner basis, convert via FGLM, compute triangular decomposition (triangMH), then compute floating point approximations with triang_solve(L,precision). Alternatively use solve(i,precision,displayflag) to compute all solutions (with multiplicities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove multiplicities by computing the radical before numeric solving
rubrics_metrics.description: To remove multiplicities, compute the radical ideal first (k = std(radical(i))) and then solve the radical ideal to get the distinct solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute std(radical(i)), then call solve(k,precision,'nodisplay') (or triang_solve) to obtain distinct complex solutions without multiplicity. Example: vdim(si) gives number of solutions with multiplicity, vdim(j) after saturation or radical gives reduced counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monomial ordering recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular offers a variety of monomial orderings. Recommendation: use dp for computations in K[x1,...,xn] (or ds for Loc(x)K[x...]) if you are not familiar with monomial orderings; for inhomogeneous input, standard/groebner computations are generally faster with the orderings Wp/Ws if the input is quasihomogeneous; if the output needs to be 'triangular' use lex (or lexicographic block-orderings) but these are usually much less efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to dp for general work. If input is quasihomogeneous, consider Wp/Ws to speed standard/groebner basis computations. If you need triangular output, use lp (lex), but expect much larger computational cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation rules for vectors, modules and rank
rubrics_metrics.description: A vector in Singular is always an element of a free module and internally represented as f1*gen(1)+...+fn*gen(n); a vector v=[f1,...,fn] should be considered as a column vector and the last 0-entries are lost in the sparse internal representation. To create a module with larger rank than given by its generators, use attrib(M,'rank',r) or define a matrix first and convert it into a module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that sparse representation causes trailing zeros to be omitted; use attrib to force rank or define matrices explicitly. Conversions between modules and matrices preserve rank and number of generators when done correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of std, dim, vdim and syz with modules
rubrics_metrics.description: std(M) computes a standard basis of M (thus gives another representation of N = R^n / M). However dim(M) and vdim(M) return dim(R^n / M) and dim_k(R^n / M). The function syz(M) returns the first syzygy module of M (the module of relations of the given generators of M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret results knowing that many functions operate on N = R^n / M rather than on M itself; consult the description of each function to determine which module is used by that function (e.g., res numbering refers to a resolution of N = R^n / M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module ordering choices affect printed vector format
rubrics_metrics.description: Module orderings give either priority to coefficients or to components. If the ordering gives priority to the component (starts with c), vectors are printed in bracket format [v1,...,vr]. Otherwise the output is v1*gen(1)+...+vr*gen(r) with gen(i) being special ring variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose module ordering among (<,C), (C,<), (<,c), (c,<) to control whether output uses bracket format or gen(...) format. Examples illustrate the different outputs for the same vectors under different module orderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix (M-) orderings representation and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Any monomial ordering can be represented by an integer matrix M (rows M1,...,Mn). The M-ordering is defined by comparing M a and M b lexicographically. Product orderings and orderings with extra weight vectors can also be represented by matrices; use M(m) or intmat to set such orderings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an intmat m and call ring r = 0,(vars),M(m) to use a custom matrix-ordering. The manual gives many example matrices for standard/global/local/weighted and product orderings to reproduce common orderings.
